He was taken to District Mortuary, Ghaziabad by the police, where his postmortem was conducted.
In connection with the accident, FIR no. 543/14, under Sections 279/338/427/304-A IPC was registered at PS Loni, Ghaziabad, U.P.

It has been alleged that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by respondent no.1/ Saleem and the said offending vehicle was registered in the name of respondent no.1/ Kapil Pal and was possessed by respondent no.3/ Shahid at the time of accident.
With these submissions, petitioners claimed a compensation of Rs.30 lakhs along with interest @ 12% per annum from date of the accident till its realization.
3. In response to the notice of the petition, respondent nos.1 and 2 appeared and filed their written statements.

Respondent no.3 failed to appear despite service of notice of petition and was proceeded ex-parte by my learned predecessor vide order dated 08.07.2016.
4.

Eventually, respondent no.3 Shahid was the owner of the offending vehicle on the date of accident and since, his driver/ respondent no.2 Saleem caused the accident and as such, they both are jointly and severally liable to pay the compensation.

9. I heard the arguments advanced by learned counsel for the parties and perused the evidence as well as other material placed on record.

My findings on the issues are as under:
i).

Whether respondent no.2 was driving vehicle, bearing no. HR20P-6987 on 06.04.2014 at 12:00 noon, in front of Delhi International School, Loni Boarder,
Ghaziabad, at high speed and in rash and negligent manner and hit against the motorcycle, bearing no. DL-14SB-2395, as a result, its occupant namely Amit Kumar fell down and sustained injuries and succumbed to the injuries?
OPD 10.
It is settled law that in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

Reference may be made to the judgments titled as New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Sakshi Bhutani & Others., MAC APP. No. 550/2011 decided on 02.07.2012, Bimla Devi & Others v.

sentences.text: On the aspect of involvement of the offending vehicle as well as rash and negligent driving of it by respondent no.2, the relevant witness examined by the petitioners is the eye-witness PW2 Sunil Kumar, the elder brother of deceased.

PW2 testified that on 06.04.2014 at about 12:00 noon, he along with his younger brother Amit Kumar (since deceased) was going to Surajmal Vihar, Delhi from Loni by motorcycle no. DL14SB- 2359, which was being driven by the deceased at a normal speed and on the correct side of the road.

He further deposed that when they reached in front of Delhi International School, Loni Border, Ghaziabad, an Eicher Tractor, bearing registration no.
HR20P- 6987, being driven by its driver at a very high speed, rashly and negligently, came from back side and hit the motorcycle with a great force.

PW2 further deposed that as a result of the accident, he fell down on the left side of the road and his younger brother towards right side of the road and came under the wheel of tractor and sustained fatal injuries and died on the spot.
He was taken to District Mortuary, Ghaziabad, by the police, where his postmortem was conducted.

The eye-witness categorically stated that this accident was caused due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of Eicher tractor and FIR no.543/2014, u/s 279/338/427/304-A IPC was registered in the matter at PS Loni.

12. The eye-witness PW2 was cross-examined at length by learned counsel for the respondent no.1 and it may be observed that during the entire cross-examination, nothing came on record _____________________________________________________________ to challenge the testimony of this witness and the only relevant suggestion on this issue put to the witness was that no incident was ever happened in his presence on 06.04.2014.
However, this suggestion was promptly denied by the eye-witness.
13. Having gone through the entire deposition of the eye witness, I find that his testimony has remained consistent and unshaken during the cross-examination.
Further, respondents did not lead any evidence to prove the defence taken in their written statements that driver/ respondent no.2 did not cause the accident.

The evidence of eye-witness (PW2) on the aspect of rash and negligent act of respondent no.2 while driving the offending vehicle has remained unimpeached and hence, the same is to be accepted on its face value itself.

14. Further, the respondent no.2, driver of the offending vehicle was the best witness, who could have stepped into the witness box to challenge the testimony of eye-witness (PW2) regarding the above accident and its manner but he preferred not to enter into the witness box during the course of inquiry.

Thus, an adverse inference is liable to be drawn against him to the effect that the accident in question occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by him in view of the law laid down in case of Cholamandalam M.S. General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kamlesh, 2009 (3) AD (Delhi) 310.
15.

19. Thus, this Tribunal is of the opinion that petitioners have been able to prove on the basis of preponderance of probabilities that the accident had occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by respondent no.2 and that resulted into death of Amit Kumar.

COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION :
21. Section 168 of the Act enjoins the Claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to be just and reasonable.
It has to be borne in mind that the compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.

22. In Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121, the relevant guidelines were laid down for death cases, which have been reiterated by the Constitution Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in a case titled as National Insurance Company vs.
Pranay Sethi & Ors.

"18.
There will be lesser need for detailed evidence.

It will also be easier for the insurance companies to Premwati vs Kapil Pal (Regd. Owner) on 21 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19551990/

19. To have uniformity and consistency, the Tribunals should determine compensation in cases of death, by the following well-settled steps:
Step-1 (Ascertaining the multiplicand)
The income of the deceased per annum should be determined.
Out of the said income a deduction should be made in regard to the amount which the deceased would have spent on himself by way of personal and living expenses.
The balance which is considered to be the contribution to the dependent family, constitutes the multiplicand.
Step-2 (Ascertaining the multiplier)
Having regard to the age of the deceased and period of active career, the appropriate multiplier should be selected.
This does not mean ascertaining the number of years he would have lived or worked but for the accident.
Having regard to several imponderables in life and economic factors, a table of multipliers with reference to the age has been identified by this Court.
The multiplier should be chosen from the said table with reference to the age of the deceased.
Step-3 (Actual Calculation)

The annual contribution to the family(multiplicand)
when multiplied by such multiplier gives the 'loss of dependency' to the family.
Thereafter, a conventional amount in the range of Rs.5,000/- to Rs.10,000/- may be added as loss of estates.
Where the deceased is survived by his widow, another conventional amount in the range of Rs.5,000 to Rs.10,000 should be added under the head of loss of consortium.

But no amount is to be awarded under the head of p a i n , s u f f e r i n g o r h a r d s h i p c a u s e d t o t h e l e g a l h e i r s o f t h e _____________________________________________________________ deceased.
The funeral expenses, cost of transportation of the body (if incurred) and the cost of any medical treatment of the deceased before death (if incurred) should also be added."

Therefore, in view of the aforesaid judgment, it is essential to take into consideration the following parameters:-

25.
An appropriate multiplier has to be determined for computation of compensation.
The judgment titled as Sarla Verma v. DTC (2009) 6 SCC 121 is relevant to consider the multiplier.

In Para 21 of the judgment, the guidelines for the multiplier were laid down in accordance with age are as under:-

The age of deceased was 22 years at the time of accident.

Future Prospects:

This issue was considered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Pranay Sethi & Others (Supra).

Relevant parts of the judgment are reproduced here as under:
_____________________________________________________________ "(iii) While determining the income, an addition of 50% of actual salary to the income of the deceased towards future prospects, where the deceased had a permanent job and was below the age of 40 years, should be made.
The addition should be 30%, if the age of the deceased was between 40 to 50 years.
In case the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years, the addition should be 15%.
Actual salary should be read as actual salary less tax.
(iv) In case the deceased was self-employed or on a fixed salary, an addition of 40% of the established income should be the warrant where the deceased was below the age of 40 years.
An addition of 25% where the deceased was between the age of 40 to 50 years and 10% where the deceased was between the age of 50 to 60 years should be regarded as the necessary method of computation.
The established income means the income minus the tax component.

(viii) Reasonable figures on conventional heads, namely, loss of estate, loss of consortium and funeral expenses should be Rs. 15,000/-, Rs.
40,000/- and Rs.15,000/- respectively.
The aforesaid amounts should be enhanced at the rate of 10% in every three years."
The deceased can be considered a self-employed.
In view of the above said judgment, an addition of 40% of the income of deceased (aged below 40 years) has to be considered towards future prospects.

Deduction towards Personal Living Expenses:
27. PW1, mother of deceased, deposed that deceased was survived by his parents,
who are the only legal heirs of deceased, and that deceased was unmarried at the time of accident.

With respect to deductions towards personal living expenses of a b a c h e l o r , t h e H o n ' b l e S u p r e m e C o u r t i n t h e c a s e o f P r a n a y S e t h i _____________________________________________________________ & Others (Supra) laid down the guiding principle as under:
"31.
Where the deceased was a bachelor and the claimants are the parents, the deduction follows a different principle.
In regard to bachelors, normally 50% is deducted as personal and living expenses, because it is assumed that a bachelor would tend to spend more on himself.

Even otherwise, there is also the possibility of his getting married in a short time, in which event the contribution to the parent(s)
and siblings is likely to be cut drastically.

Further, subject to evidence to the contrary,
the father is likely to have his own income and will not be considered as a dependent Premwati vs Kapil Pal (Regd. Owner) on 21 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19551990/
10 and the mother alone will be considered as a dependent.

In the absence of evidence to the contrary, brothers and sisters will not be considered as dependents, because they will either be independent and earning, or married, or be dependent on the father."
28.
Therefore, in this case, 50% of the income of the deceased is to be deducted towards his personal living expenses.

LIABILITY :
32.
Now, the question arises as to which of the respondents is liable to pay the compensation amount.

Admittedly, the offending vehicle was not insured at the time of accident and therefore, the respondent no.2 Saleem, being driver of the offending vehicle is the principal tort feasor whereas,
the respondent no.1 Kapil Pal, being registered owner would have the vicarious liability.

33. However, learned counsel for respondent no.1 Kapil Pal contended that respondent no.1 had sold the offending vehicle to Mr. Rajbir on 06.05.2009 i.e. much prior to the date of accident which occurred on 06.04.2014.

In support of his said contention, respondent no.1 examined RW1 Mr.
Saurabh Makkar, who stated that respondent no.1 had sold the offending tractor to Mr. Rajbir.

However, on perusal of said affidavits,
I find no mention about the presence of this witness at the time of execution thereof.

Moreover,
during cross-examination, this witness himself admitted that it is nowhere mentioned in the affidavits that he was present when the same were executed.

Further, respondent no.1 Kapil Pal got examined himself as RW2, through Local Commissioner,
on direction of this Tribunal.

Further, it has been deposed by RW2 Kapil Pal that the fact that Shahid had purchased the tractor is corroborated by zimni dated 13.06.2014 but he neither examined the Investigating Officer nor Shahid (who was proceeded ex-parte) to prove the said fact on record.
36.
It is evident from the record that respondent no.1 Kapil Pal was the registered owner of the offending vehicle at the time of accident on 06.04.2014.
This fact also finds strength from the admission of RW2 Kapil Pal, who stated during his cross- examination that he had purchased the offending tractor in the year 2008.

Further, copy of the particulars of the offending vehicle obtained from Registering Authority, M.V. cum SDO (C), Hisar placed on record shows Kapil Pal as the registered owner of the offending tractor and its registration date as 19.03.2008.
Thus, it is clear that in record of the Registering Authority, the respondent no.1 Kapil Pal was the registered owner on the date of accident.

37. In a situation such as the present where the registered owner has purported to transfer the vehicle but continues to be reflected in the records of the registering authority as the owner of the vehicle, he would not stand absolved of liability.

In case of Naveen Kumar vs. Vijay Kumar & Ors.,
CA No.1427/2018, decided on 06.02.2018, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that:
"Parliament has consciously introduced the definition of the expression 'owner' in Section 2(30) of M.V. Act making a departure from the provisions of Section _____________________________________________________________ 2(19) in the earlier Act of 1939

entities.text:
Naveen Kumar vs. Vijay Kumar & Ors.,
CA No.1427/2018
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: , the principle underlying the provisions of Section 2(30) is that the victim of a motor accident or in the case of a death, the legal heirs of the deceased victim should not be left in a state of uncertainty.

A claimant for compensation ought not to be burdened with following a trail of successive transfers,
which are not registered with the registering authority.
To hold otherwise would be to defeat the salutary object and purpose of the Act."

Also, it has been well settled by Hon'ble Supreme Court in catena of judgments that for the purposes of M.V. Act, the person whose name is reflected in the records of the registering authority is the 'owner' within the meaning of Section 2(30) of the said Act, is liable to compensate.

Thus,
respondent No.1 Kapil Pal would remain liable to pay the compensation.

Resultantly, the respondent no.1 Kapil Pal (registered owner) and respondent no. 2 Saleem (driver) would be liable to pay the compensation amount to the petitioners and their liability would remain joint and several.

It is settled law that in an action founded on the principle of fault liability, the proof of rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle is sine qua non.
However, the standard of proof is not as strict as applied in criminal cases and evidence is to be tested on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
Holistic view is to be taken while dealing with the Claim Petition based upon negligence.
Strict rules of evidence are not applicable in an inquiry conducted by the Claims Tribunal.

General Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Kamlesh, 2009 (3) AD (Delhi) 310.

COMPUTATION OF COMPENSATION :
21. Section 168 of the Act enjoins the Claims Tribunal to hold an inquiry into the claim to make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to be just and reasonable.
It has to be borne in mind that the compensation is not expected to be a windfall or a bonanza nor it should be pittance.
22. In Sarla Verma and Others v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Anr. (2009) 6 Supreme Court Cases 121, the relevant guidelines were laid down for death cases, which have been reiterated by the Constitution Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in a case titled as National Insurance Company vs.
Pranay Sethi & Ors.
19. To have uniformity and consistency, the Tribunals should determine compensation in cases of death, by the following well-settled steps:
Step-1 (Ascertaining the multiplicand)
The income of the deceased per annum should be determined.
Out of the said income a deduction should be made in regard to the amount which the deceased would have spent on himself by way of personal and living expenses.
The balance which is considered to be the contribution to the dependent family, constitutes the multiplicand.
Having regard to the age of the deceased and period of active career, the appropriate multiplier should be selected.
This does not mean ascertaining the number of years he would have lived or worked but for the accident.
Thus, the income of the deceased would be considered to be Rs.10,374/- per month.
An appropriate multiplier has to be determined for computation of compensation.
Also, it has been well settled by Hon'ble Supreme Court in catena of judgments that for the purposes of M.V. Act, the person whose name is reflected in the records of the registering authority is the 'owner' within the meaning of Section 2(30) of the said Act, is liable to compensate.
